issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s assertions of ownership and transferable rights cause forfeiture only when, viewed in their context, they clearly and unequivocally disclaim the landlord’s title.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a government-owned plot held by the claimant and his predecessors under a tenancy whose original terms were unclear; the appeal proceeded on the assumption that it was a permanent tenancy with heritable and transferable rights.

In a compensation claim, the claimant described the land as belonging to him and himself and his ancestors as owners exercising permanent, heritable and transferable rights, while also referring to the Government’s consent and seeking a court declaration of his interest.
The claimant sought a declaration that he had rights as owner or, alternatively, as a permanent lessee, and did not dispute his liability to pay rent.
The Government treated the assertions as repudiation of its title and gave notice of forfeiture; the High Court upheld the finding of forfeiture.
issues.conclusion: The assertions, considered in their context, were not a clear and unequivocal disclaimer of the Government’s title and did not forfeit the tenancy, assuming it was a permanent tenancy. The appeal was allowed and the matter remanded to the High Court for further proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 111(g), embodies the rule that a lease may be determined by forfeiture when a lessee renounces the tenancy by setting up a third party’s title or claiming title in himself. Although that Act did not apply to the area, the principle applies to such tenancies as a matter of justice, equity and good conscience: Maharaja of Jeypore v. Rukmini Pattamahadevi, 46 Ind App 109 (AIR 1919 PC 1). A disclaimer must be clear and unequivocal and made to the landlord’s knowledge. A claim to rights greater than the tenant’s actual rights does not by itself amount to disclaimer; the words must be assessed in the context of the tenancy and the document as a whole, as illustrated by Prag Narain v. Kadir Bakhsh, ILR 35 All 145. The English rule in Vivian v. Moat, (1881) 16 Ch D 730, does not govern Indian tenancies; an assertion in a pleading, including an inadvertent one, does not cause forfeiture unless it is a clear and unequivocal renunciation.

rule.if: lease_forfeiture_dispute and permanent_tenancy_assumed and assertions_read_in_context and (assertions_not_clear_unequivocal or landlord_interest_acknowledged)

predicates.lease_forfeiture_dispute: The proceeding concerned whether a landlord had forfeited a tenant’s interest because of the tenant’s statements about ownership.
predicates.permanent_tenancy_assumed: The appeal proceeded on the assumption that the tenant held a permanent tenancy with heritable and transferable rights.
predicates.assertions_read_in_context: The court assessed the tenant’s ownership statements in light of the history and circumstances of the tenancy and the documents as a whole.
predicates.assertions_not_clear_unequivocal: The tenant’s statements did not clearly and unequivocally renounce the tenancy or deny the landlord’s title.
predicates.landlord_interest_acknowledged: The tenant referred to the landlord’s consent, continued to accept liability for rent, and claimed rights as a lessee in the alternative.

issues.definition: When a forfeiture dispute concerns an assumed permanent tenancy and the tenant’s statements, read in context, are not a clear and unequivocal disclaimer or acknowledge the landlord’s interest, forfeiture is not established.
